  1052	\subsection{Generalized Pauli observables}
  1053	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
  1054	
  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational
  1102	basis $\{\ket{j}\}_{j \in \F_q}$.
  1103	To map this basis to the common eigenbasis of the $\qp^X$ operators, one can
  1104	apply the Fourier transform
  1105	\begin{equation}
  1106	  \label{eq:fourier-f}
  1107	  F \,=\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b\in \Fq} \omega^{-\tr(ab)}
  1108	  \ket{a}\bra{b}\;.
  1109	\end{equation}
  1110	Explicitly, the eigenbases consist of the vectors $\ket{e_W}$ labeled by an
  1111	element $e \in \Fq$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
  1112	\begin{equation*}
  1113	  \ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_j \omega^{- \tr(e j)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
  1114	  \ket{e_Z}   = \ket{e}\;.
  1115	\end{equation*}
  1116	We denote the POVM whose elements are projectors onto basis vectors of the
  1117	eigenbasis associated with the observables $\qp^W$ by $\{\qp^W_e\}_e$.
  1118	Then for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a\in \Fq$, the observables $\qp^W(a)$ can be
  1119	written as
  1120	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1121	  \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(a b)} \qp^W_b\;.
  1122	\end{equation}
  1123	
  1124	To invert this relation, we first quote the following useful Fourier fact.
  1125	\begin{lemma}[Fact 3.2 of \cite{NW19}]
  1126	  \label{lem:cancellation}
  1127	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F^k$. For all $v \not\in V^\perp$, 
  1128	  \begin{equation*}
  1129	    \E_{u \sim V} \omega^{\tr(u \cdot v)} = 0\;,
  1130	  \end{equation*}
  1131	  where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $u$ from $V$.
  1132	\end{lemma}
  1133	
  1134	We may now invert~\Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}:
  1135	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single}
  1136	  \E_{a\in \F_q} \omega^{-\tr(ab)} \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b'\in \F_q} \E_{a\in \F_q}
  1137	  \omega^{\tr(a(b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;,
  1138	\end{equation}
  1139	where the second step follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation}.
  1140	
  1141	For systems with many qudits, we will consider tensor products of the operators
  1142	$\qp^W$.
  1143	Slightly abusing notation, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$ and $a \in \Fq^n$ we denote by
  1144	$\qp^W(a)$ the tensor product $\qp^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \qp^W(a_n)$.
  1145	These obey the twisted commutation relations
  1146	\begin{equation*}
  1147	  \forall a,b\in \Fq^n,\qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) \,=\, \omega^{-\tr (a \cdot
  1148	    b)}\, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;,
  1149	\end{equation*}
  1150	where $a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i \in \Fq$.
  1151	For $W\in\{X,Z\}$ and $e \in \Fq^n$ define the eigenstates
  1152	\[ \ket{e_W} = \ket{(e_1)_W} \ot \dots \ot \ket{(e_n)_W}\;, \]
  1153	and associated rank-$1$ projectors $\qp^W_e$. Analogous versions of \Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1154	and \Cref{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single} relate the multi-qubit observables
  1155	and projectors:
  1156	\begin{align}
  1157	  \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b \in \Fq^n} \omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}
  1158	  \qp^W_b\;, \label{eq:pauli-obs-proj} \\
  1159	    \E_{a\in \F_q^n} \omega^{-\tr(a \cdot b)} \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b'\in \F_q^n} \E_{a\in \F_q^n}
  1160	  \omega^{\tr(a\cdot (b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;. \label{eq:pauli-inversion-0}
  1161	\end{align}
  1162	
  1163	Since we only consider finite fields $\F_q$ such that $q = 2^k$ the maximally
  1164	entangled state $\ket{\EPR_q}$ and the corresponding qudit Pauli
  1165	observables/projectors are isomorphic to a tensor product of maximally entangled
  1166	states $\ket{\EPR_2}$ and \emph{qubit} Pauli observables/projectors
  1167	respectively; this is shown in the next lemma.
  1168	This is used to argue that the Pauli basis test (described in
  1169	Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier}) gives a self-test for Pauli observables and
  1170	maximally entangled states over qubits.
  1171	
  1172	\begin{lemma}
  1173	  \label{lem:pauli-binary}
  1174	  For all admissible field sizes $q = 2^k$ and integers $L$, there exists
  1175	  an isomorphism $\phi: (\C^q)^{\otimes L} \to (\C^2)^{\otimes L k}$
  1176	  such that\footnote{ Here we have applied the natural identifications between
  1177	  $(\C^q)^{\ot L} \ot (\C^q)^{\ot L}$ and $(\C^q \ot \C^q)^{\ot L}$,
  1178	  and between $(\C^2)^{\ot L k} \ot (C^2)^{\ot Lk}$ and $(\C^2 \ot
  1179	  \C^2)^{\ot Lk}$.}
  1180	\begin{equation}
  1181	    \label{eq:epr-q-to-epr-2}
  1182	    \phi \otimes \phi \, \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes L} =
  1183	    \ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes L k}\;.
  1184	  \end{equation}
  1185	  Moreover, for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and for all $u \in \F_q^L$
  1186		\begin{equation}
  1187		\label{eq:pauli-q-to-pauli-2}
  1188	  	\tau^W_u = \phi^\dagger\, \Bigl (\bigotimes_{i=1}^L
  1189	    \bigotimes_{j=1}^{k} \sigma^{W}_{u_{ij}} \Bigr) \, \phi\;.

\subsection{Linear spaces}
\label{sec:linear-spaces}

Linear spaces considered in the paper generally take the form $V = \F^n$ for a
finite field $\F$ and integer $n \geq 1$.
In particular, when we write ``let $V$ be a linear space'', unless explicitly
stated otherwise we always mean a space of the form $\F^n$.
Let $\hat{E} = \{ \hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_2, \ldots, \hat{e}_n\}$ denote the standard basis of $V$, where for
$i \in\{ 1, 2, \ldots, n\}$,
\begin{equation*}
  \hat{e}_i = (0, \ldots, 0, 1, 0, \ldots, 0)
\end{equation*}
has a $1$ in the $i$-th coordinate and $0$'s elsewhere.
We write $\End(V)$ to denote the set of linear transformations from $V$ to
itself.
\begin{definition}[Register subspace]
  A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
  subset of the standard basis of $V$.\footnote{The use of the term ``register''
    is meant to create an analogy for how the space of multiple qubits is often
    partitioned into ``registers'' containing a few qubits each.}
  We often represent such a subspace as an indicator vector $u\in \{0,1\}^s$,
  where $s=\dim(V)$, such that if $\{\hat{e}_1,\ldots,\hat{e}_s\}$ is the standard basis of
  $V$ then $S = \text{span}\{\hat{e}_i|\,u_i=1\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
  Let $\hat{E} = \{ \hat{e}_i\}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$.
  For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$, $v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V$,
  define the \emph{dot product}
  \begin{equation*}
    u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
  \end{equation*}
  Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. The \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
  \begin{equation*}
    S^\perp \,=\, \big\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0
    \text{ for all }  v \in S \big\}\;.
  \end{equation*}
  Although the notation $S^\perp$ does not explicitly refer to $V$, the ambient
  space will always be clear from context.
\end{definition}

We note that over finite fields, the notion of orthogonality does not possess
all of the same intuitive properties of orthogonality over fields such as $\R$
or $\C$; for example, a non-zero subspace $S$ may be orthogonal to itself (e.g.\
$\mathrm{span} \{ (1,1) \}$ over $\F_2$).
However, the following remains true over all fields.

\begin{lemma}
  \label{lem:perp_perp}
  Suppose $S$ is a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) =
  \dim(V)$, and 
  \begin{equation*}
    (S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
  \end{equation*}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
  The statement about the dimensions follows from the fact that vectors in $S^\perp$ are
  the solution to a feasible linear system of equations with $\dim(S)$ linearly
  independent rows; this implies that the solution space has dimension exactly
  $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$.
  Next, we argue that $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
  Let $u \in S$.
  Since all vectors $v \in S^\perp$ are orthogonal to every vector in $S$,
  in particular $u$, this implies that $u \in (S^\perp)^\perp$.
  By dimension counting, it follows that $(S^\perp)^\perp = S$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}\label{def:complementary}
  Given a linear space $V$, two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of $V$ are said to form a
  pair of \emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
\begin{equation*}
  S \cap T = \{ 0 \}, \quad S + T = V\;.
\end{equation*}
In this case, we write $V = S \oplus T$.
Any $x\in V$ can be written as $x = x^S + x^T$ for $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$
in a unique way.
We refer to $x^S$ (resp.~$x^T$) as the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel
  to $T$} (resp.~\emph{onto $T$ parallel to $S$}).
We call the unique linear map $L: V \to V$ that maps $x \mapsto x^S$ the
\emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
\end{definition}

A given subspace may have many different complementary subspaces: consider the
example of $S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1) \}$ in $\F_2^2$.
Different complementary subspaces include $T = \mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and
$T' = \mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$.
It is convenient to define the notion of a \emph{canonical complement} of a
subspace $S$, given a basis for $S$.

\begin{definition}
  \label{def:canonical-complement}
  Let $E$ be the standard basis of linear space $V = \F^n$.
  Let $F = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly
  independent vectors in $V$.
  The \emph{canonical complement $F^\perp$ of $F$} is the set of $n-m$ independent
  vectors defined as follows.
  Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i, j}\, \hat{e}_j$.

  fields, transform the $m\times n$ matrix $(a_{i, j})$ to reduced row echelon
  form $(b_{i, j})$.
  Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices of the leading $1$ entry in each row
  of $(b_{i, j})$.
  The canonical complement is defined as $F^\perp = \{ \hat{e}_j : j \not\in J \}$.
\end{definition}


\begin{remark}
We emphasize that the canonical complement $F^\perp$ is a \emph{set} (rather than
a subspace), and it is defined with respect to a \emph{set} of linearly
independent vectors $F$. While there are equivalent ways of defining
a canonical complement of a \emph{subspace} in a basis-independent manner, 
we use this particular definition because it makes it clear that
the canonical complement of a set $F$ is efficiently computable. 
\end{remark}

+/-!
+# Executable Gauss-Jordan elimination
+
+This module develops the algorithmic part of paper `def:canonical-complement`.
+Matrices are materialized as vectors of vectors: evaluating an entry of an
+intermediate matrix never repeats an earlier field operation. Columns are
+processed from left to right, with the first available nonzero row as pivot.
+
+The computational data are field operations and decidable equality. Arithmetic
+operation counts use unit cost for field operations and equality tests, without
+asserting bit complexity for an arbitrary field representation.
+
+`gaussianElimination_correct` proves RREF and row-span correctness for arbitrary
+input rows. `gaussianElimination_of_linearIndependent` gives the source's
+independent-row case. `gaussianElimination_cost_le_poly` bounds the actual
+program's charged arithmetic and zero tests by `n * (m + n + 2*m*n)`.
+
+## References
+
+* `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:303-333`,
+  Definition `def:canonical-complement` and its efficiency remark.
+* Issue #690, continuing the algorithmic obligation of issue #676.
+-/
+
+open scoped BigOperators
+
+namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
+
+namespace GaussianElimination
+
+variable {K : Type*} {m n : ℕ}
+
+/-- Array-backed storage for a finite matrix. This is computational storage for
+Mathlib matrices, not a different algebraic notion of matrix. -/
+abbrev StoredMatrix (K : Type*) (m n : ℕ) := Vector (Vector K n) m
+
+/-- Read a stored matrix as a Mathlib matrix. -/
+def toMatrix (A : StoredMatrix K m n) : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin n) K :=
+  fun i j => A[i.val][j.val]
+
+/-- Evaluate each entry once and store the resulting matrix. -/
+def ofMatrix (A : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin n) K) : StoredMatrix K m n :=
+  Vector.ofFn fun i => Vector.ofFn fun j => A i j
+
+@[simp] lemma toMatrix_ofMatrix (A : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin n) K) :
+    toMatrix (ofMatrix A) = A := by
+  funext i j
+  simp [toMatrix, ofMatrix]
+
+variable [Field K]
+
+/-- Tabulate counted computations, evaluating each computation once. Reading the
+stored results and summing their natural-number costs perform no field operations. -/
+def tabulateCounted {α : Type*} {k : ℕ} (f : Fin k → α × ℕ) : Vector α k × ℕ :=
+  let samples := Vector.ofFn f
+  (samples.map Prod.fst, ∑ i : Fin k, samples[i.val].2)
+
+/-- Counted pivot elimination. A division costs one field operation; each
+nonpivot entry uses one multiplication and one subtraction. The normalized
+pivot row is stored before it is used by the other rows. -/
+def eliminateColumnCounted (A : StoredMatrix K m n) (r s : Fin m) (c : Fin n) :
+    StoredMatrix K m n × ℕ :=
+  let B := fun i j => toMatrix A (Equiv.swap r s i) j
+  let v := tabulateCounted fun j => (B r j / B r c, 1)
+  let result := tabulateCounted fun i =>
+    if i = r then (v.1, 0)
+    else tabulateCounted fun j => (B i j - B i c * v.1[j.val], 2)
+  (result.1, v.2 + result.2)
+
+/-- Swap the selected row into position `r`, normalize it, and clear its column
+in every other row. Both the normalized row and the result are materialized. -/
+def eliminateColumn (A : StoredMatrix K m n) (r s : Fin m) (c : Fin n) :
+    StoredMatrix K m n :=
+  (eliminateColumnCounted A r s c).1
+
+/-- Entrywise formula for the materialized pivot step. -/
+lemma eliminateColumn_apply (A : StoredMatrix K m n) (r s i : Fin m) (c j : Fin n) :
+    toMatrix (eliminateColumn A r s c) i j =
+      if i = r then toMatrix A s j / toMatrix A s c
+      else toMatrix A (Equiv.swap r s i) j -
+        toMatrix A (Equiv.swap r s i) c * (toMatrix A s j / toMatrix A s c) := by
+  by_cases hi : i = r <;>
+    simp [eliminateColumn, eliminateColumnCounted, tabulateCounted, toMatrix, hi]
+
+/-- A pivot step with a nonzero pivot preserves the entire row span. The inverse
+row expressions recover the swapped input rows from the normalized pivot row. -/
+theorem eliminateColumn_span (A : StoredMatrix K m n) (r s : Fin m) (c : Fin n)
+    (hc : toMatrix A s c ≠ 0) :
+    Submodule.span K (Set.range (toMatrix (eliminateColumn A r s c)).row) =
+      Submodule.span K (Set.range (toMatrix A).row) := by
+  let B := toMatrix (eliminateColumn A r s c)
+  have hp : B.row r = (toMatrix A s c)⁻¹ • (toMatrix A).row s := by
+    ext j
+    simp [B, Matrix.row, eliminateColumn_apply, div_eq_mul_inv, mul_comm]
+  have hi (i : Fin m) (hir : i ≠ r) :
+      B.row i = (toMatrix A).row (Equiv.swap r s i) -
+        toMatrix A (Equiv.swap r s i) c • B.row r := by
+    ext j
+    simp [B, Matrix.row, eliminateColumn_apply, hir]
+  have hrow (i : Fin m) : (toMatrix A).row i ∈
+      Submodule.span K (Set.range (toMatrix A).row) := Submodule.subset_span ⟨i, rfl⟩
+  have hnew (i : Fin m) : B.row i ∈ Submodule.span K (Set.range B.row) :=
+    Submodule.subset_span ⟨i, rfl⟩
+  have hpr : B.row r ∈ Submodule.span K (Set.range (toMatrix A).row) := by
+    rw [hp]
+    exact Submodule.smul_mem _ _ (hrow s)
+  apply le_antisymm
+  · apply Submodule.span_le.mpr
+    rintro _ ⟨i, rfl⟩
+    by_cases hir : i = r
+    · subst i
+      exact hpr
+    · rw [hi i hir]
+      exact Submodule.sub_mem _ (hrow _) (Submodule.smul_mem _ _ hpr)
+  · apply Submodule.span_le.mpr
+    rintro _ ⟨i, rfl⟩
+    have hs : (toMatrix A).row s = toMatrix A s c • B.row r := by
+      rw [hp, smul_smul, mul_inv_cancel₀ hc, one_smul]
+    by_cases his : i = s
+    · subst i
+      rw [hs]
+      exact Submodule.smul_mem _ _ (hnew r)
+    · have hswap : Equiv.swap r s i ≠ r := by
+        intro h
+        apply his
+        simpa using congrArg (Equiv.swap r s) h
+      have hback : (toMatrix A).row i =
+          B.row (Equiv.swap r s i) + toMatrix A i c • B.row r := by
+        rw [hi _ hswap, Equiv.swap_apply_self]
+        exact (sub_add_cancel _ _).symm
+      rw [hback]
+      exact Submodule.add_mem _ (hnew _) (Submodule.smul_mem _ _ (hnew r))
+
+/-- The arithmetic count of the actual materialized pivot step is bounded by
+`n + 2*m*n`. The estimate permits charging the pivot row as an additional
+eliminated row; no search or matrix evaluation is hidden in a field operation. -/
+theorem eliminateColumnCounted_cost (A : StoredMatrix K m n)
+    (r s : Fin m) (c : Fin n) :
+    (eliminateColumnCounted A r s c).2 ≤ n + m * (2 * n) := by
+  simp only [eliminateColumnCounted, tabulateCounted, Vector.getElem_ofFn]
+  simp only [Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ, Fintype.card_fin, smul_eq_mul, mul_one]
+  apply Nat.add_le_add_left
+  calc
+    (∑ i : Fin m, (if i = r then (_, 0) else (_, n * 2)).2) ≤
+        ∑ _i : Fin m, 2 * n := by
+      apply Finset.sum_le_sum
+      intro i _
+      split_ifs <;> simp [Nat.mul_comm]
+    _ = m * (2 * n) := by simp
+
+/-- The selected column becomes a unit column. Any column in which both swapped
+rows were zero remains unchanged, preserving previously completed pivot columns. -/
+theorem eliminateColumn_entries (A : StoredMatrix K m n) (r s : Fin m) (c : Fin n)
+    (hc : toMatrix A s c ≠ 0) :
+    (∀ i, toMatrix (eliminateColumn A r s c) i c = if i = r then 1 else 0) ∧
+      ∀ j, toMatrix A r j = 0 → toMatrix A s j = 0 →
+        ∀ i, toMatrix (eliminateColumn A r s c) i j = toMatrix A i j := by
+  constructor
+  · intro i
+    rw [eliminateColumn_apply, div_self hc]
+    split_ifs <;> simp
+  · intro j hr hs i
+    rw [eliminateColumn_apply, hs, zero_div]
+    by_cases hir : i = r
+    · subst i
+      simp [hr]
+    · by_cases his : i = s
+      · subst i
+        simp [hir, hr, hs]
+      · simp [hir, Equiv.swap_apply_of_ne_of_ne hir his]
+
+variable [DecidableEq K]
+
+/-- Scan a supplied row list in order. Each inspected row is charged one zero
+test, including a conservative charge when its index is below `r` and the field
+test is skipped. The caller uses `List.finRange m`, so this is a bounded search. -/
+def findPivot (A : StoredMatrix K m n) (r : ℕ) (c : Fin n) :
+    List (Fin m) → Option (Fin m) × ℕ
+  | [] => (none, 0)
+  | i :: is =>
+    if r ≤ i.val ∧ toMatrix A i c ≠ 0 then (some i, 1)
+    else
+      let rest := findPivot A r c is
+      (rest.1, rest.2 + 1)
+
+/-- The search returns the first eligible row, and charges at most the list
+length. Its specification reuses Lean's list search rather than an existence
+oracle or enumeration of candidate reduced matrices. -/
+theorem findPivot_spec (A : StoredMatrix K m n) (r : ℕ) (c : Fin n)
+    (is : List (Fin m)) :
+    (findPivot A r c is).1 =
+        is.find? (fun i => decide (r ≤ i.val ∧ toMatrix A i c ≠ 0)) ∧
+      (findPivot A r c is).2 ≤ is.length := by
+  induction is with
+  | nil => simp [findPivot]
+  | cons i is ih =>
+    by_cases hi : r ≤ i.val ∧ toMatrix A i c ≠ 0
+    · simp [findPivot, hi]
+    · simpa [findPivot, hi] using ih
+
+/-- Computational elimination state. Only the first `rank` pivot entries are
+used; the other entries are storage that has not yet been assigned a pivot. -/
+structure State (K : Type*) (m n : ℕ) where
+  entries : StoredMatrix K m n
+  rank : ℕ
+  pivots : Vector ℕ m
+  operations : ℕ
+
+/-- Initial state, before any column has been inspected. -/
+def initialState (A : StoredMatrix K m n) : State K m n :=
+  ⟨A, 0, Vector.replicate m 0, 0⟩
+
+/-- Process one column, selecting the first available nonzero row. A column
+without a pivot leaves the matrix unchanged and still charges for its search. -/
+def step (S : State K m n) (c : Fin n) : State K m n :=
+  if hr : S.rank < m then
+    let search := findPivot S.entries S.rank c (List.finRange m)
+    match search.1 with
+    | none => { S with operations := S.operations + search.2 }
+    | some s =>
+      let result := eliminateColumnCounted S.entries ⟨S.rank, hr⟩ s c
+      ⟨result.1, S.rank + 1, S.pivots.set S.rank c.val hr,
+        S.operations + search.2 + result.2⟩
+  else S
+
+/-- Run the first `k` column iterations. Calls at `k > n` remain at the final
+state; the public algorithm calls this function at exactly `k = n`. -/
+def runColumns (A : StoredMatrix K m n) : ℕ → State K m n
+  | 0 => initialState A
+  | k + 1 =>
+    let S := runColumns A k
+    if hk : k < n then step S ⟨k, hk⟩ else S
+
+/-- Partial RREF invariant after `k` columns. Completed pivots are ordered and
+reduced; unprocessed rows vanish in the inspected columns. This is a loop
+invariant for the executable program, not an assumption on the input matrix. -/
+structure Invariant (A : StoredMatrix K m n) (k : ℕ) (S : State K m n) : Prop where
+  rank_le : S.rank ≤ m
+  pivot_lt : ∀ i : Fin m, i.val < S.rank → S.pivots[i.val] < k
+  pivot_strict : ∀ i j : Fin m, i < j → j.val < S.rank →
+    S.pivots[i.val] < S.pivots[j.val]
+  pivot_entry : ∀ t : Fin m, t.val < S.rank → ∀ c : Fin n,
+    S.pivots[t.val] = c.val → ∀ i,
+      toMatrix S.entries i c = if i = t then 1 else 0
+  zero_before : ∀ i : Fin m, i.val < S.rank → ∀ c : Fin n,
+    c.val < S.pivots[i.val] → toMatrix S.entries i c = 0
+  remaining_zero : ∀ i : Fin m, S.rank ≤ i.val → ∀ c : Fin n,
+    c.val < k → toMatrix S.entries i c = 0
+  span_eq : Submodule.span K (Set.range (toMatrix S.entries).row) =
+    Submodule.span K (Set.range (toMatrix A).row)
+  cost_le : S.operations ≤ k * (m + n + m * (2 * n))
+
+omit [DecidableEq K] in
+/-- The initial state satisfies the invariant for every matrix, including empty
+row and column index types. No independence or rank certificate is required. -/
+theorem initialState_invariant (A : StoredMatrix K m n) :
+    Invariant A 0 (initialState A) := by
+  refine ⟨Nat.zero_le _, ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_, rfl, by simp [initialState]⟩
+  · intro i hi
+    exact (Nat.not_lt_zero _ hi).elim
+  · intro i j hij hj
+    exact (Nat.not_lt_zero _ hj).elim
+  · intro t ht
+    exact (Nat.not_lt_zero _ ht).elim
+  · intro i hi
+    exact (Nat.not_lt_zero _ hi).elim
+  · intro i hi c hc
+    exact (Nat.not_lt_zero _ hc).elim
+
+/-- One column iteration preserves the partial RREF conditions and row span,
+and adds at most `m + n + 2*m*n` charged field operations and zero tests. -/

+theorem Invariant.step {A : StoredMatrix K m n} {S : State K m n} (c : Fin n)
+    (h : Invariant A c.val S) : Invariant A (c.val + 1) (step S c) := by
+  by_cases hr : S.rank < m
+  · have hsearch := findPivot_spec S.entries S.rank c (List.finRange m)
+    have hsearch_cost : (findPivot S.entries S.rank c (List.finRange m)).2 ≤ m := by
+      simpa using hsearch.2
+    cases hf : (findPivot S.entries S.rank c (List.finRange m)).1 with
+    | none =>
+      have hz (i : Fin m) (hi : S.rank ≤ i.val) : toMatrix S.entries i c = 0 := by
+        have hh := List.find?_eq_none.mp (hsearch.1.symm.trans hf) i (List.mem_finRange i)
+        simpa [hi] using hh
+      simp only [GaussianElimination.step, dif_pos hr, hf]
+      refine ⟨h.rank_le, ?_, h.pivot_strict, h.pivot_entry, h.zero_before, ?_,
+        h.span_eq, ?_⟩
+      · intro i hi
+        exact Nat.lt_succ_of_lt (h.pivot_lt i hi)
+      · intro i hi j hj
+        by_cases hjc : j.val < c.val
+        · exact h.remaining_zero i hi j hjc
+        · have heq : j = c := Fin.ext (by omega)
+          subst j
+          exact hz i hi
+      · have hc := h.cost_le
+        dsimp only
+        rw [Nat.add_mul, Nat.one_mul]
+        omega
+    | some s =>
+      have hs : S.rank ≤ s.val ∧ toMatrix S.entries s c ≠ 0 := by
+        simpa using List.find?_some (hsearch.1.symm.trans hf)
+      let r : Fin m := ⟨S.rank, hr⟩
+      have hcol := eliminateColumn_entries S.entries r s c hs.2
+      have hpres (j : Fin n) (hj : j.val < c.val) (i : Fin m) :
+          toMatrix (eliminateColumn S.entries r s c) i j = toMatrix S.entries i j :=
+        hcol.2 j (h.remaining_zero r (Nat.le_refl _) j hj)
+          (h.remaining_zero s hs.1 j hj) i
+      have hcost := eliminateColumnCounted_cost S.entries r s c
+      simp only [GaussianElimination.step, dif_pos hr, hf]
+      change Invariant A (c.val + 1)
+        ⟨eliminateColumn S.entries r s c, S.rank + 1,
+          S.pivots.set S.rank c.val hr,
+          S.operations + (findPivot S.entries S.rank c (List.finRange m)).2 +
+            (eliminateColumnCounted S.entries r s c).2⟩
+      refine ⟨by dsimp only; omega, ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_,
+        (eliminateColumn_span S.entries r s c hs.2).trans h.span_eq, ?_⟩
+      · intro i hi
+        dsimp only at hi ⊢
+        rw [Vector.getElem_set]
+        split_ifs with hir
+        · omega
+        · exact Nat.lt_succ_of_lt (h.pivot_lt i (by omega))
+      · intro i j hij hj
+        dsimp only at hj ⊢
+        have hij' : i.val < j.val := hij
+        have hir : S.rank ≠ i.val := by omega
+        simp only [Vector.getElem_set, if_neg hir]
+        split_ifs with hjr
+        · exact h.pivot_lt i (by omega)
+        · exact h.pivot_strict i j hij (by omega)
+      · intro t ht j hj i
+        dsimp only at ht hj ⊢
+        by_cases htr : S.rank = t.val
+        · have hteq : t = r := Fin.ext htr.symm
+          have hjeq : j = c := by
+            apply Fin.ext
+            simpa [Vector.getElem_set, htr] using hj.symm
+          subst t
+          subst j
+          exact hcol.1 i
+        · have ht' : t.val < S.rank := by omega
+          have hj' : S.pivots[t.val] = j.val := by
+            simpa [Vector.getElem_set, htr] using hj
+          rw [hpres j (by rw [← hj']; exact h.pivot_lt t ht') i]
+          exact h.pivot_entry t ht' j hj' i
+      · intro i hi j hj
+        dsimp only at hi hj ⊢
+        by_cases hir : S.rank = i.val
+        · have hieq : i = r := Fin.ext hir.symm
+          have hjc : j.val < c.val := by
+            simpa [Vector.getElem_set, hir] using hj
+          subst i
+          rw [eliminateColumn_apply, if_pos rfl, h.remaining_zero s hs.1 j hjc,
+            zero_div]
+        · have hi' : i.val < S.rank := by omega
+          have hj' : j.val < S.pivots[i.val] := by
+            simpa [Vector.getElem_set, hir] using hj
+          rw [hpres j (lt_trans hj' (h.pivot_lt i hi')) i]
+          exact h.zero_before i hi' j hj'
+      · intro i hi j hj
+        dsimp only at hi hj ⊢
+        by_cases hjc : j.val < c.val
+        · rw [hpres j hjc i]
+          exact h.remaining_zero i (by omega) j hjc
+        · have hjeq : j = c := Fin.ext (by omega)
+          subst j
+          rw [hcol.1, if_neg]
+          intro hir
+          have := congrArg Fin.val hir
+          dsimp [r] at this
+          omega
+      · dsimp only
+        have hc := h.cost_le
+        rw [Nat.add_mul, Nat.one_mul]
+        omega
+  · simp only [GaussianElimination.step, dif_neg hr]
+    refine ⟨h.rank_le, ?_, h.pivot_strict, h.pivot_entry, h.zero_before, ?_,
+      h.span_eq, ?_⟩
+    · intro i hi
+      exact Nat.lt_succ_of_lt (h.pivot_lt i hi)
+    · intro i hi j hj
+      have := i.isLt
+      omega
+    · have hc := h.cost_le
+      rw [Nat.add_mul, Nat.one_mul]
+      omega
+
+/-- Induction over the bounded column loop derives the invariant from the input
+matrix alone. In particular, correctness certificates are not program inputs. -/
+theorem runColumns_invariant (A : StoredMatrix K m n) (k : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ n) :
+    Invariant A k (runColumns A k) := by
+  induction k with
+  | zero => exact initialState_invariant A
+  | succ k ih =>
+    have hkn : k < n := by omega
+    rw [runColumns, dif_pos hkn]
+    exact (ih (by omega)).step ⟨k, hkn⟩
+
+/-- The computed nonpivot indices. Only assigned pivot entries are inspected;
+the finite scan uses integer comparisons and no field operations. -/
+def State.nonpivotIndices (S : State K m n) : Finset (Fin n) :=
+  Finset.univ.filter fun j => ∀ i : Fin m, i.val < S.rank → S.pivots[i.val] ≠ j.val
+
+end GaussianElimination
+
+open GaussianElimination
+
+variable {K : Type*} [Field K] [DecidableEq K] {m n : ℕ}
+
+/-- Deterministic, materialized Gauss-Jordan elimination. The input is stored
+matrix data, with field operations and decidable equality supplied by the caller.
+Exactly `n` bounded column iterations are executed. This constructs the reduced
+matrix and nonpivot indices used in paper `def:canonical-complement`. -/
+def gaussianElimination (A : StoredMatrix K m n) : State K m n :=
+  runColumns A n
+
+/-- The computed nonzero rows. The bound used to index storage is proved by the
+loop invariant, rather than supplied by the caller. No field arithmetic occurs
+when this view of the stored output is read. -/
+def gaussianEliminationRows (A : StoredMatrix K m n) :
+    Matrix (Fin (gaussianElimination A).rank) (Fin n) K :=
+  let S := gaussianElimination A
+  let h := runColumns_invariant A n (Nat.le_refl n)
+  fun i => toMatrix S.entries ⟨i.val, lt_of_lt_of_le i.isLt h.rank_le⟩
+
+/-- Increasing pivot embedding read from the computed pivot array. The bound and
+ordering proofs are consequences of the loop invariant and are erased at run time. -/
+def gaussianEliminationPivots (A : StoredMatrix K m n) :
+    Fin (gaussianElimination A).rank ↪o Fin n :=
+  let S := gaussianElimination A
+  let h := runColumns_invariant A n (Nat.le_refl n)
+  OrderEmbedding.ofStrictMono
+    (fun i => ⟨S.pivots[i.val]'(lt_of_lt_of_le i.isLt h.rank_le),
+      h.pivot_lt ⟨i.val, lt_of_lt_of_le i.isLt h.rank_le⟩ i.isLt⟩)
+    (by
+      intro i j hij
+      exact h.pivot_strict ⟨i.val, lt_of_lt_of_le i.isLt h.rank_le⟩
+        ⟨j.val, lt_of_lt_of_le j.isLt h.rank_le⟩ hij j.isLt)
+
+/-- Correctness of the executable elimination program for arbitrary input rows.
+Its nonzero rows satisfy conventional RREF, span exactly the input row space,
+and its computed nonpivot indices are the existing canonical complement. The
+other stored rows are zero. This supplies the construction in paper
+`def:canonical-complement`; the independent-row specialization follows below. -/
+theorem gaussianElimination_correct (A : StoredMatrix K m n) :
+    IsReducedRowEchelon (gaussianEliminationRows A) (gaussianEliminationPivots A) ∧
+      Submodule.span K (Set.range (gaussianEliminationRows A).row) =
+        Submodule.span K (Set.range (toMatrix A).row) ∧
+      (∀ i : Fin m, (gaussianElimination A).rank ≤ i.val →
+        (toMatrix (gaussianElimination A).entries).row i = 0) ∧
+      canonicalComplement (Submodule.span K (Set.range (toMatrix A).row)) =
+        (gaussianElimination A).nonpivotIndices := by
+  let S := gaussianElimination A
+  have h : Invariant A n S := runColumns_invariant A n (Nat.le_refl n)
+  have hB : IsReducedRowEchelon (gaussianEliminationRows A)
+      (gaussianEliminationPivots A) := by
+    constructor
+    · intro i j
+      have he := h.pivot_entry ⟨j.val, lt_of_lt_of_le j.isLt h.rank_le⟩ j.isLt
+        (gaussianEliminationPivots A j) rfl ⟨i.val, lt_of_lt_of_le i.isLt h.rank_le⟩
+      simpa only [gaussianEliminationRows, Fin.ext_iff] using he
+    · intro i j hj
+      exact h.zero_before ⟨i.val, lt_of_lt_of_le i.isLt h.rank_le⟩ i.isLt j hj
+  have hz (i : Fin m) (hi : S.rank ≤ i.val) : (toMatrix S.entries).row i = 0 := by
+    funext j
+    exact h.remaining_zero i hi j j.isLt
+  have hspan : Submodule.span K (Set.range (gaussianEliminationRows A).row) =
+      Submodule.span K (Set.range (toMatrix A).row) := by
+    rw [← h.span_eq]
+    apply le_antisymm
+    · apply Submodule.span_le.mpr
+      rintro _ ⟨i, rfl⟩
+      exact Submodule.subset_span ⟨⟨i.val, lt_of_lt_of_le i.isLt h.rank_le⟩, rfl⟩
+    · apply Submodule.span_le.mpr
+      rintro _ ⟨i, rfl⟩
+      by_cases hi : i.val < S.rank
+      · exact Submodule.subset_span ⟨⟨i.val, hi⟩, rfl⟩
+      · rw [hz i (Nat.le_of_not_lt hi)]
+        exact Submodule.zero_mem _
+  refine ⟨hB, hspan, hz, ?_⟩
+  rw [← hspan, hB.canonicalComplement_eq_nonpivot_indices]
+  ext j
+  simp only [State.nonpivotIndices, Finset.mem_compl, Finset.mem_image,
+    Finset.mem_univ, true_and, Finset.mem_filter]
+  constructor
+  · intro hj i hi heq
+    apply hj
+    refine ⟨⟨i.val, hi⟩, ?_⟩
+    exact Fin.ext heq
+  · rintro hj ⟨i, hi⟩
+    exact hj ⟨i.val, lt_of_lt_of_le i.isLt h.rank_le⟩ i.isLt (congrArg Fin.val hi)
+
+/-- For the independent rows of paper `def:canonical-complement`, all `m` output
+rows are pivot rows. The full stored output is RREF with the input row span,
+and its computed nonpivot indices are precisely the source complement. The only
+effectivity data beyond the paper's field are executable operations and equality. -/
+theorem gaussianElimination_of_linearIndependent (A : StoredMatrix K m n)
+    (hA : LinearIndependent K (toMatrix A).row) :
+    (gaussianElimination A).rank = m ∧
+      ∃ pivot : Fin m ↪o Fin n,
+        IsReducedRowEchelon (toMatrix (gaussianElimination A).entries) pivot ∧
+          Submodule.span K (Set.range (toMatrix (gaussianElimination A).entries).row) =
+            Submodule.span K (Set.range (toMatrix A).row) ∧
+          canonicalComplement (Submodule.span K (Set.range (toMatrix A).row)) =
+            (gaussianElimination A).nonpivotIndices := by
+  have hc := gaussianElimination_correct A
+  have h := runColumns_invariant A n (Nat.le_refl n)
+  have hin := finrank_span_eq_card hA
+  have hout := finrank_span_eq_card hc.1.linearIndependent_rows
+  rw [hc.2.1] at hout
+  simp only [Fintype.card_fin] at hin hout
+  have hrank : (gaussianElimination A).rank = m := hout.symm.trans hin
+  let e := (Fin.castOrderIso hrank.symm).toOrderEmbedding
+  refine ⟨hrank, e.trans (gaussianEliminationPivots A), ?_, h.span_eq, hc.2.2.2⟩
+  constructor
+  · intro i j
+    have he := hc.1.pivot_entry (e i) (e j)
+    simpa [gaussianEliminationRows, e, Fin.ext_iff] using he
+  · intro i j hj
+    exact hc.1.zero_before (e i) j hj
+
+/-- Polynomial arithmetic-operation bound for the executable program, including
+its pivot searches. Each of the `n` columns charges at most `m` zero tests, `n`
+divisions, and `2*m*n` multiplications/subtractions. Short-circuited zero tests
+may be overcharged. Counts come from the same materialized computations as the
+matrix output, not from a separate nominal loop counter.
+
+Array access and storage use no field operations. Tabulation, cost summation,
+row scanning, and pivot-array updates make bounded passes of sizes at most
+`m`, `n`, and `m*n` per column. The result is an arithmetic bound under unit-cost
+field operations/equality, not a bit-complexity claim about a field encoding. -/
+theorem gaussianElimination_cost_le_poly (A : StoredMatrix K m n) :
+    (gaussianElimination A).operations ≤ n * (m + n + m * (2 * n)) :=
+  (runColumns_invariant A n (Nat.le_refl n)).cost_le
+
+end MIPStarRE.QPBT

+# Executable canonical elimination
+
+## Result and Source
+
+`MIPStarRE/QPBT/Algebra/RowEchelonAlgorithm.lean` supplies the remaining
+algorithmic construction for Definition `def:canonical-complement` in
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:303-333`. The source transforms
+independent coordinate rows to reduced row echelon form by a canonical
+Gaussian-elimination algorithm and selects the standard vectors in nonpivot
+columns. Its following remark asserts efficient computation, without specifying
+an exponent or a bit representation for field elements.
+
+The new program chooses columns from left to right and chooses the first
+available nonzero row in each column. Its output satisfies the predecessor's
+`IsReducedRowEchelon` predicate and has exactly the original row span.
+Its computed nonpivot indices equal the existing `canonicalComplement`.
+Its charged field arithmetic and zero tests are bounded by
+
+```text
+n * (m + n + 2*m*n).
+```
+
+All these results are proved from input data. No RREF certificate, invariant,
+row-span identity, complement equality, or complexity bound is a caller
+hypothesis. No proof hole remains in the new module. The result is ready for
+independent review; this audit does not change blueprint completion marks,
+paper-gap statuses, or the project's completion disposition.
+
+## Program and Mathematical Proof
+
+`StoredMatrix K m n` is an array-backed `Vector (Vector K n) m`.
+`toMatrix` reads it as a Mathlib matrix. `ofMatrix` materializes a Mathlib
+matrix, and `toMatrix_ofMatrix` proves that all its entries are preserved.
+The storage type therefore does not change the underlying linear algebra.
+
+For a selected column `c`, `findPivot` scans the finite list of row indices
+in increasing order. An eligible row has index at least the number of
+completed pivots and has a nonzero entry in column `c`. `findPivot_spec`
+identifies the result with Lean's `List.find?` and bounds the number of
+charged tests by the list length. There is no unbounded search or enumeration
+of candidate matrices.
+
+Let `r` be the next pivot position and `s` the selected row. Write `B` for
+the input with rows `r` and `s` interchanged. The pivot step stores the row
+`v[j] = B[r,j] / B[r,c]`, then stores `v` in row `r` and
+`B[i,j] - B[i,c] * v[j]` in every other row. The normalized row is evaluated
+before it is used to compute the other rows. Later entry access consequently
+does not repeat its field operations.
+
+`eliminateColumn_span` proves both span inclusions. Each output row is a
+linear combination of input rows. Conversely, multiply the normalized pivot
+row by the original nonzero pivot to recover the selected input row, and add
+the removed multiple back to each other row. `eliminateColumn_entries`
+proves that column `c` becomes a unit column and that a column zero in both
+swapped rows stays unchanged.
+
+The loop invariant records ordered pivot columns with identity entries,
+zeros before each completed pivot, zeros in inspected columns of unprocessed
+rows, equality of row spans, and the accumulated cost bound. The initial
+state satisfies it for every input matrix. `Invariant.step` proves its
+preservation in the pivot, unsuccessful-search, and exhausted-row cases;
+`runColumns_invariant` then proves it after all columns have been processed.
+This invariant is proved internally, not attached to the source hypotheses.
+
+`gaussianElimination_correct` proves that the computed nonzero rows are in
+conventional RREF and span the input row space, while all remaining stored
+rows vanish. It applies the predecessor's
+`IsReducedRowEchelon.canonicalComplement_eq_nonpivot_indices` to identify the
+computed nonpivot set. `gaussianElimination_of_linearIndependent` additionally
+proves that the computed rank is `m` and that the full stored matrix is RREF.
+The rank equality follows because an independent finite family has dimension
+equal to its cardinality, applied to both row families with their proved
+common span. This uses Mathlib's `finrank_span_eq_card`.
+
+The pivot embedding and reduced-row view read the computed arrays. Their
+index bounds and ordering proofs come from the loop invariant and are erased
+at execution. They do not select an abstract RREF witness. The predecessor's
+abstract RREF existence theorem is not used in the new construction.
+
+## Cost Model
+
+The input is materialized field data, with executable field operations and
+`DecidableEq K`. A field division, multiplication, subtraction, and equality
+test each have unit arithmetic cost. No claim about bit complexity or the
+internal implementation of a supplied field operation is made.
+
+`tabulateCounted` evaluates each computation once into an array of value/count
+pairs. It reads these stored values to construct the result and sums the
+stored natural-number counts. The normalized row uses `n` divisions. Each
+other row uses `n` multiplications and `n` subtractions. The proved bound for
+one actual pivot computation is `n + m*(2*n)`; this conservatively allows
+charging the pivot row as another eliminated row.
+
+Every inspected search row is charged one zero test. If an index comparison
+already rejects that row, the omitted field test is still charged. Thus the
+counter is an upper bound on field operations and tests, not a claim that
+every charged test was executed. At most `m` rows are inspected per column.
+The same column program accumulates these search charges and the counts from
+the materialized pivot computations. The invariant bounds this actual counter
+after `k` columns by `k*(m+n+m*(2*n))`.
+`gaussianElimination_cost_le_poly` specializes the bound at `k = n`.
+
+The representation also accounts for access and materialization. Array reads
+perform no field arithmetic. Per column, list construction and search make
+bounded passes of size `m`; normalized-row tabulation and count summation have
+size `n`; result tabulation and count summation have size at most `m*n`.
+Updating the pivot array requires at most a copy of `m` indices. There are
+exactly `n` column iterations, including the constant-work exhausted-row cases.
+Extracting the nonpivot set compares at most `m*n` stored natural numbers.
+These finite passes give polynomial administrative work in the usual
+unit-cost array model. The formal numeric theorem counts field operations and
+zero tests; it is not a machine-instruction or memory-allocation theorem.
+
+`ofMatrix` evaluates each of the `m*n` supplied entries once. The elimination
+bound starts with stored input; it does not purport to bound arbitrary
+computation hidden in a user-supplied function producing matrix entries.
+

+It scans columns from left to right, searches a bounded list for the first

+by the nonzero pivot, and clears its column in every other row. The normalized
+row and resulting matrix are stored before subsequent use.

+## Cost Model and Verdict
+
+Each field division, multiplication, subtraction, and equality test has unit
+cost. `tabulateCounted` first evaluates each entry computation into a stored
+value/count pair, then reads these pairs to extract values and sum their
+charges. The normalized pivot row costs `n` divisions. Clearing the remaining
+rows costs at most `2*m*n` operations, conservatively including the pivot
+row in that upper bound. Every inspected search row costs one test, even when
+an index comparison short-circuits the field test. There are at most `m`
+inspected rows per column.
+
+The program accumulates those charges as it constructs the matrices.

+arbitrary computation within an external entry-producing function is outside

+tabulation, summation of counts, and pivot updates. The nonpivot selection

+no formal instruction-count, memory-allocation, or field-encoding theorem.

1	\chapter{Algebraic preliminaries for the Pauli basis test}
     2	\label{chap:qpbt-algebra}
     3	
     4	This chapter records the algebraic preliminaries needed for the quantum Pauli
     5	basis test, following the preliminaries of \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}: subspace
     6	machinery over finite fields (which underlies the conditionally linear question
     7	distributions of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-games}), field extensions, traces, and
     8	self-dual bases, the low-degree code, lines in $\F_q^m$, and the generalized
     9	Pauli observables together with the EPR states they act on. Measurements,
    10	strategies, and consistency relations for nonlocal games are treated in
    11	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-games}; the test itself is defined in
    12	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}.
    13	
    14	\section{Linear spaces and subspaces}
    15	% Paper label sec:linear-spaces kept for cross-reference fidelity.
    16	\label{sec:linear-spaces}
    17	
    18	Linear spaces are always of the form $V = \F^n$ for a finite field $\F$ and an
    19	integer $n \ge 1$, unless explicitly stated otherwise. We write $\hat{E} =
    20	\{\hat{e}_1, \dots, \hat{e}_n\}$ for the standard basis of $V$, where
    21	$\hat{e}_i$ has a $1$ in the $i$-th coordinate and $0$'s elsewhere, and
    22	$\mathrm{End}(V)$ for the set of linear maps from $V$ to itself.
    23	
    24	\begin{definition}[Register subspace]\label{def:register-subspace}
    25		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.registerSubmodule}
    26		\leanok
    27		A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
    28		subset of the standard basis of $V$. Such a subspace is represented by an
    29		indicator vector $u \in \{0,1\}^s$, where $s = \dim(V)$, via
    30		$S = \mathrm{span}\{\hat{e}_i : u_i = 1\}$.
    31	\end{definition}
    32	
    33	% The dot product itself is Mathlib's `dotProduct`; the Lean declaration listed here
    34	% is the orthogonal-subspace half of the node, which is the part this development
    35	% defines for itself.
    36	\begin{definition}[Dot product and orthogonal subspace]\label{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    37		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.dotOrthogonal}
    38		\leanok
    39		For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$ and
    40		$v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V = \F^n$, the \emph{dot product} is
    41		\[
    42			u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
    43		\]
    44		For a subspace $S$ of $V$, the \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
    45		\[
    46			S^\perp = \bigl\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0 \text{ for all } v \in S \bigr\}\;.
    47		\]
    48		The notation $S^\perp$ leaves the ambient space $V$ implicit.
    49	\end{definition}
    50	
    51	Over finite fields, orthogonality lacks some of the familiar properties it has
    52	over $\R$ or $\C$; for example, a nonzero subspace may be orthogonal to itself,
    53	as is $\mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ over $\F_2$. The following dimension identity
    54	nevertheless holds over every field.
    55	
    56	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:perp_perp}
    57		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.finrank_add_finrank_dotOrthogonal, MIPStarRE.QPBT.dotOrthogonal_dotOrthogonal}
    58		\leanok
    59		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    60		Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) = \dim(V)$, and
    61		\[
    62			(S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
    63		\]
    64	\end{lemma}
    65	\begin{proof}
    66		\leanok
    67		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    68		The elements of $S^\perp$ are the solutions of a feasible linear system whose
    69		coefficient matrix has $\dim(S)$ linearly independent rows, so the solution
    70		space has dimension exactly $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$. Every $u \in S$ is
    71		orthogonal to every element of $S^\perp$, so $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
    72		Applying the dimension identity twice shows that
    73		$\dim\bigl((S^\perp)^\perp\bigr) = \dim(S)$, so the inclusion is an equality.
    74	\end{proof}
    75	
    76	\begin{definition}[Complementary subspaces]\label{def:complementary}
    77		Two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of a linear space $V$ form a pair of
    78		\emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
    79		\[
    80			S \cap T = \{0\}\;, \qquad S + T = V\;.
    81		\]
    82		In this case we write $V = S \oplus T$. Every $x \in V$ can be written
    83		uniquely as $x = x^S + x^T$ with $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$; we call $x^S$
    84		(resp.\ $x^T$) the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel to $T$} (resp.\
    85		onto $T$ parallel to $S$). The unique linear map $L : V \to V$ with
    86		$x \mapsto x^S$ is the \emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
    87	\end{definition}
    88	
    89	A subspace may have many complementary subspaces: in $\F_2^2$, the subspace
    90	$S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ has the distinct complements
    91	$\mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and $\mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$. Given a basis of $S$,
    92	one may nevertheless single out a \emph{canonical} complement.
    93	
    94	\begin{definition}[Deterministic Gaussian elimination]\label{def:gaussian-elimination}
    95	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.gaussianElimination}
    96	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.GaussianElimination.eliminateColumnCounted}
    97	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.GaussianElimination.State.nonpivotIndices}
    98	  \leanok
    99	  This auxiliary construction specifies the Gaussian elimination used in
   100	  Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}; it is not a separate labelled
   101	  definition of \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. Let $K$ be any field with executable
   102	  field operations and decidable equality, and let $A\in K^{m\times n}$ be
   103	  given by its stored entries, where $m,n\geq 0$.
   104	
   105	  In this construction, rows $a\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and columns
   106	  $b\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ use the paper's numbering. They correspond to the
   107	  formal indices $i=a-1$ and $j=b-1$, respectively. A pivot in paper row
   108	  $a$ has column number
   109	  $p_{\mathrm{paper}}(a)=p_{\mathrm{Lean}}(a-1)+1$.
   110	  The same conversion applies to every row or column subscript below.
   111	  The number $r$ of completed pivots is a count in both conventions:
   112	  the next paper row is $r+1$, with formal index $r$.
   113	
   114	  Start with $B=A$ and $r=0$, and process columns $b=1,\ldots,n$ in order.
   115	  When $r<m$, inspect the rows in increasing order and choose the first
   116	  $s>r$ with $B_{s,b}\ne 0$. If there is no such row, leave $B$ unchanged.
   117	  Otherwise interchange rows $r+1$ and $s$, writing $D$ for the resulting
   118	  matrix, and form the stored row
   119	  \[
   120	    v_d=D_{r+1,d}/D_{r+1,b}\qquad(1\leq d\leq n).
   121	  \]
   122	  Replace $B$ by the stored matrix
   123	  \[
   124	    B'_{a,d}=\begin{cases}
   125	      v_d,&a=r+1,\\
   126	      D_{a,d}-D_{a,b}v_d,&a\ne r+1,
   127	    \end{cases}
   128	  \]
   129	  record $p_{\mathrm{paper}}(r+1)=b$, and increase $r$ by one.
   130	  Once $r=m$, subsequent columns leave the state unchanged. The output
   131	  consists of $B$, the count $r$, the recorded pivot columns, and their
   132	  complement in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Each normalized row is stored before
   133	  forming the other rows, so reading it does not repeat its divisions.
   134	\end{definition}
   135	
   136	% Issues #676 and #690: the intrinsic correspondence and executable construction
   137	% are both proved. The efficiency assertion uses unit-cost field arithmetic and
   138	% equality tests, as specified in thm:gaussian-elimination-cost.
   139	% See audits/2026-09-22_issue-690-canonical-integration.md; no exemption is granted.
   140	\begin{definition}[Canonical complement]\label{def:canonical-complement}
   141		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.canonicalComplement}
   142	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.gaussianElimination}
   143	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.gaussianElimination_of_linearIndependent}
   144	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.gaussianElimination_cost_le_poly}
   145	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.IsReducedRowEchelon.canonicalComplement_eq_nonpivot_indices}
   146	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.IsReducedRowEchelon.pivot_indices_eq_of_span_eq}
   147	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.card_canonicalComplement_span_rows}
   148	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.linearIndependent_canonicalComplement}
   149	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.canonicalComplement_registerSubmodule}
   150	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.registerSubmodule_canonicalComplement_eq_dotOrthogonal}
   151	  \leanok
   152		\uses{def:register-subspace, def:gaussian-elimination}
   153		Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$ and let
   154		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly independent
   155		vectors. Write $v_a = \sum_{b=1}^n A_{a,b}\, \hat{e}_b$, and, using a
   156		canonical Gaussian-elimination algorithm valid over arbitrary fields,
   157		transform the $m \times n$ matrix $A$ to reduced row echelon form
   158		$B$. Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices containing the leading
   159		$1$ entry of each row of $B$. The \emph{canonical complement of $F$}
   160		is the set of $n - m$ standard basis vectors
   161		\[
   162			F^\perp = \{\hat{e}_b : b \notin J\}\;.
   163		\]
   164		The canonical complement is a \emph{set} of vectors, not a subspace.
   165		Although defined through the basis $F$, it depends only on
   166		$\mathrm{span}(F)$ and the ambient standard basis. Indeed, if $\pi_k$ is
   167		restriction to the first $k$ coordinates, the number of pivots among those
   168		coordinates is $\dim\pi_k(\mathrm{span}(F))$. Thus $b$ is a nonpivot
   169		coordinate precisely when
   170		\[
   171			\dim\pi_b(\mathrm{span}(F)) = \dim\pi_{b-1}(\mathrm{span}(F))\;,
   172		\]
   173		which is independent of the chosen basis and its order. The presentation
   174		through Gaussian elimination, adopted by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, makes the
   175		canonical complement efficiently computable. If $S$ is a register subspace
   176		spanned by $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$, then the canonical complement of
   177		$\hat{E}_0$ is $\hat{E} \setminus \hat{E}_0$, and its span coincides with
   178		$S^\perp$.
   179	
   180	  Definition~\ref{def:gaussian-elimination} gives a deterministic realization
   181	  of this construction. Theorem~\ref{thm:gaussian-elimination-correct}
   182	  identifies its computed nonpivot indices with the intrinsic complement.
   183	  For stored input, Theorem~\ref{thm:gaussian-elimination-cost} gives at most
   184	  $n(m+n+2mn)$ charged field operations and equality tests, with each such
   185	  operation assigned unit cost. This is the arithmetic interpretation of
   186	  efficient construction over an arbitrary field; it makes no assertion
   187	  about the bit complexity of a field representation.
   188	\end{definition}
   189	
   190	The row indices $a=1,\ldots,m$ and column indices $b=1,\ldots,n$ here and
   191	in the following decomposition use the one-based numbering of
   192	\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. Their zero-based counterparts in Lean are $i=a-1$ and
   193	$j=b-1$, respectively; the matrix entry $A_{a,b}$ corresponds to the entry
   194	at $(i,j)$. If $p_a=p_{\mathrm{paper}}(a)$ is the pivot column of row $a$
   195	and $p_{\mathrm{Lean}}$ is the zero-based pivot map, then
   196	\[
   197	  p_{\mathrm{paper}}(a)=p_{\mathrm{Lean}}(a-1)+1\;.
   198	\]
   199	The prefix lengths $b$ and $b-1$ therefore become $j+1$ and $j$; a prefix
   200	length counts coordinates and is not itself a coordinate index. In particular,
   201	$\pi_0$ restricts to the empty prefix. Similarly, a row sum
   202	$\sum_{a=1}^m$ becomes the sum of the reindexed terms over
   203	$i\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$.

   205	\begin{theorem}[Correctness of Gaussian elimination]\label{thm:gaussian-elimination-correct}
   206	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.gaussianEliminationRows}
   207	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.gaussianEliminationPivots}
   208	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.gaussianElimination_correct}
   209	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.gaussianElimination_of_linearIndependent}
   210	  \leanok
   211	  \uses{def:gaussian-elimination, def:canonical-complement}
   212	  This auxiliary theorem verifies the construction in
   213	  Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}. For any stored matrix
   214	  $A\in K^{m\times n}$ over a field with the computational data of
   215	  Definition~\ref{def:gaussian-elimination}, let $B,r,p$ be the computed
   216	  matrix, number of pivots, and pivot columns, in the paper's numbering.
   217	  The first $r$ rows of $B$ are in reduced row echelon form:
   218	  $p(1)<\cdots<p(r)$, $B_{a,p(c)}=\delta_{ac}$ for $1\leq a,c\leq r$,
   219	  and $B_{a,b}=0$ for $b<p(a)$. Every remaining row is zero, and
   220	  \[
   221	    \mathrm{span}\{B_{a,*}:1\leq a\leq r\}
   222	      =\mathrm{span}\{A_{a,*}:1\leq a\leq m\}=:S.
   223	  \]
   224	  The computed nonpivot columns are exactly those $b$ for which
   225	  $\dim\pi_b(S)=\dim\pi_{b-1}(S)$, where $\pi_k$ restricts to the first
   226	  $k$ coordinates. Thus paper column $b$ corresponds to formal column
   227	  $j=b-1$, and the two prefix lengths are $j+1$ and $j$.
   228	  If the input rows are independent, then $r=m$, the full output matrix
   229	  is in reduced row echelon form, and its nonpivot standard basis vectors
   230	  are precisely $F^\perp$ for $F=\{A_{1,*},\ldots,A_{m,*}\}$.
   231	\end{theorem}
   232	\begin{proof}
   233	  \leanok
   234	  \uses{def:gaussian-elimination, def:canonical-complement}
   235	  After each inspected column, the completed pivots are ordered unit
   236	  columns, their rows vanish before their pivots, and the remaining rows
   237	  vanish in all inspected columns. A nonzero pivot step preserves the row
   238	  span: its normalization and row subtractions can be reversed. Induction
   239	  over the columns proves these assertions for the output. Removing the
   240	  zero rows preserves its span. The prefix-dimension characterization of
   241	  Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement} then identifies the nonpivot
   242	  columns. For independent input rows, equality of row spans gives
   243	  $r=\dim S=m$.
   244	\end{proof}

   246	\begin{theorem}[Arithmetic cost of Gaussian elimination]\label{thm:gaussian-elimination-cost}
   247	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.GaussianElimination.tabulateCounted}
   248	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.GaussianElimination.findPivot_spec}
   249	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.GaussianElimination.eliminateColumnCounted_cost}
   250	  \lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.gaussianElimination_cost_le_poly}
   251	  \leanok
   252	  \uses{def:gaussian-elimination}
   253	  This auxiliary theorem makes precise the arithmetic cost of the
   254	  construction accompanying Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   255	  Give each field division, multiplication, subtraction, and equality test
   256	  unit cost. For every stored $m\times n$ matrix, the charged cost $C(A)$ of
   257	  Definition~\ref{def:gaussian-elimination} satisfies
   258	  \[
   259	    C(A)\leq n(m+n+2mn).
   260	  \]
   261	  The counter accompanies the actual stored computations: each tabulation
   262	  evaluates an entry once and then sums its stored charge. Each inspected
   263	  search row is charged one equality test, even if its index already
   264	  excludes it and the field test is omitted. This conservative convention
   265	  makes $C(A)$ an upper bound on the executed field operations and tests.
   266	\end{theorem}
   267	\begin{proof}

     3	/-!
     4	# Reduced row echelon form and the canonical complement
     5	
     6	For matrices with independent rows, reduced row echelon form consists of ordered
     7	pivot columns, an identity matrix in those columns, and zeros before each pivot.
     8	This module compares its nonpivot indices with the intrinsic prefix-rank
     9	definition of `canonicalComplement`.
    10	
    11	Independent input rows have such a matrix with the same row span and an
    12	invertible change of row basis. The pivot index set depends only on that span.
    13	An explicit row combination gives the complementary-subspace decomposition.
    14	The canonical complement has the asserted cardinality and independence, and
    15	for register subspaces it consists of the remaining standard basis vectors.
    16	
    17	The arbitrary-field and zero-dimensional cases are extensions of the paper's
    18	ambient convention of a finite field and positive ambient dimension. The results
    19	include an executable decomposition once an RREF matrix is supplied, but do not
    20	provide an executable elimination algorithm or a complexity theorem for finding it.
    21	
    22	## References
    23	
    24	* `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:219-222`, ambient convention.
    25	* `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:303-373`,
    26	  Definition `def:canonical-complement` and Lemma `lem:canonical-complement`.
    27	* `audits/2026-09-21_issue-676-canonical-complement-alignment.md`, issue #676.
    28	-/

    42	  pivot_entry : ∀ i j, B i (pivot j) = if i = j then 1 else 0

    50	  apply Fintype.linearIndependent_iff.mpr
    51	  intro c hc i

    59	    {B : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin n) K} {pivot : Fin m ↪o Fin n}
    60	    (hB : IsReducedRowEchelon B pivot) {k : ℕ} (hk : k ≤ n) :
    61	    prefixRank (Submodule.span K (Set.range B.row)) k hk =
    62	      (Finset.univ.filter fun i => (pivot i).val < k).card := by
    63	  classical
    64	  let s := Finset.univ.filter fun i => (pivot i).val < k
    65	  let b : s → Fin k → K := fun i => prefixMap k n hk (B.row i.val)
    66	  have hb : LinearIndependent K b := by
    67	    apply Fintype.linearIndependent_iff.mpr
    68	    intro c hc i
    69	    have hi := congrFun hc
    70	      ⟨(pivot i.val).val, (Finset.mem_filter.mp i.property).2⟩
    71	    simp only [Finset.sum_apply, Pi.smul_apply, smul_eq_mul] at hi
    72	    change (∑ j : s, c j * B j.val (pivot i.val)) = 0 at hi
    73	    simpa [hB.pivot_entry, ← Subtype.ext_iff] using hi
    74	  have hspan :
    75	      Submodule.span K (Set.range (fun i => prefixMap k n hk (B.row i))) =
    76	        Submodule.span K (Set.range b) := by
    77	    apply le_antisymm
    78	    · apply Submodule.span_le.mpr
    79	      rintro _ ⟨i, rfl⟩
    80	      by_cases hi : (pivot i).val < k
    81	      · exact Submodule.subset_span ⟨⟨i, Finset.mem_filter.mpr ⟨Finset.mem_univ _, hi⟩⟩,
    82	          rfl⟩
    83	      · have hz : prefixMap k n hk (B.row i) = 0 := by
    84	          funext j
    85	          apply hB.zero_before
    86	          change j.val < (pivot i).val
    87	          exact lt_of_lt_of_le j.isLt (Nat.le_of_not_lt hi)
    88	        change prefixMap k n hk (B.row i) ∈ _
    89	        rw [hz]
    90	        exact Submodule.zero_mem _
    91	    · apply Submodule.span_mono
    92	      rintro _ ⟨i, rfl⟩
    93	      exact ⟨i.val, rfl⟩
    94	  rw [prefixRank, Submodule.map_span, ← Set.range_comp]
    95	  change Module.finrank K
    96	    (Submodule.span K (Set.range (fun i => prefixMap k n hk (B.row i)))) = s.card
    97	  rw [hspan, finrank_span_eq_card hb]
    98	  exact Fintype.card_coe s

     3	/-!
     4	# Subspaces for the Pauli basis test
     5	
     6	This module supplies the register subspaces, dot-product orthogonals, and the
     7	canonical coordinate complement used by the conditionally linear maps.  The
     8	canonical complement is presented through the intrinsic pivot-rank test; the
     9	equivalence with a particular row-reduced-echelon implementation is a later
    10	construction theorem.
    11	
    12	## References
    13	
    14	The statement-level definitions are blueprint `def:register-subspace`,
    15	`def:dot-product-orthogonal`, `def:canonical-complement`, and
    16	`def:cl-canonical`;
    17	the paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:231-384`.
    18	
    19	Note: this module contributes declarations to the comparator statement closure
    20	of the QPBT headline theorems, which must elaborate in the same environment as
    21	the Mathlib-only `ChallengeQPBT.lean`.  Keep the full `import Mathlib`; do not
    22	narrow it.  See `docs/comparator.md`, "Environment alignment".
    23	-/
    24	
    25	open scoped BigOperators
    26	
    27	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    28	
    29	variable {K ι : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    30	
    31	/--
    32	`registerSubmodule K S` is the span of the standard coordinate vectors indexed
    33	by `S`.  It is the Lean encoding of blueprint `def:register-subspace`, whose
    34	paper origin is
    35	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:231-239`.
    36	-/
    37	def registerSubmodule (K : Type*) [Field K] (S : Finset ι) : Submodule K (ι → K) :=
    38	  Submodule.span K {v | ∃ i, i ∈ S ∧ v = Pi.single i 1}
    39	
    40	/--
    41	`dotOrthogonal W` consists of vectors whose coordinate dot product with every
    42	member of `W` vanishes.  This is blueprint
    43	`def:dot-product-orthogonal`, with paper origin
    44	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:241-255`.
    45	-/
    46	def dotOrthogonal (W : Submodule K (ι → K)) : Submodule K (ι → K) where
    47	  carrier := {u | ∀ v, v ∈ W → dotProduct u v = 0}
    48	  zero_mem' := by
    49	    intro v hv
    50	    simp [dotProduct]
    51	  add_mem' := by
    52	    intro u v hu hv w hw
    53	    calc
    54	      dotProduct (u + v) w =
    55	          (dotProduct u w) + (dotProduct v w) := by
    56	            change (∑ i, (u i + v i) * w i) =
    57	              (∑ i, u i * w i) + (∑ i, v i * w i)
    58	            simp_rw [add_mul]
    59	            rw [Finset.sum_add_distrib]
    60	      _ = 0 := by rw [hu w hw, hv w hw, add_zero]
    61	  smul_mem' := by
    62	    intro c u hu v hv
    63	    calc
    64	      dotProduct (c • u) v = c * dotProduct u v := by
    65	        simp [dotProduct, smul_eq_mul, mul_assoc, Finset.mul_sum]
    66	      _ = 0 := by rw [hu v hv, mul_zero]
    67	
    68	/-- Restrict a coordinate vector to the first `k` coordinates.  Lean-only rank
    69	infrastructure for blueprint
    70	`def:canonical-complement`, paper `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:231-384`.
    71	-/
    72	def prefixMap (k n : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ n) :
    73	    (Fin n → K) →ₗ[K] (Fin k → K) :=
    74	  { toFun := fun x i => x ⟨i.1, lt_of_lt_of_le i.2 hk⟩
    75	    map_add' := by
    76	      intro x y
    77	      rfl
    78	    map_smul' := by
    79	      intro c x
    80	      rfl }
    81	
    82	/-- The rank of a prefix restriction used by the pivot characterization. -/
    83	noncomputable def prefixRank {n : ℕ} (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K))
    84	    (k : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ n) : ℕ :=
    85	  Module.finrank K (W.map (prefixMap k n hk))
    86	
    87	/-- For a row matrix, prefix rank is the matrix rank after retaining the first
    88	`k` columns. This is Lean-only infrastructure for comparing
    89	`canonicalComplement` with the reduced-row-echelon construction in blueprint
    90	`def:canonical-complement`, paper
    91	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:303-320`. -/
    92	lemma prefixRank_span_rows_eq_rank_submatrix {m n k : ℕ}
    93	    (A : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin n) K) (hk : k ≤ n) :
    94	    prefixRank (Submodule.span K (Set.range A.row)) k hk =
    95	      (A.submatrix id (Fin.castLE hk)).rank := by
    96	  have himage :
    97	      (prefixMap (K := K) k n hk) '' Set.range A.row =
    98	        Set.range (A.submatrix id (Fin.castLE hk)).row := by
    99	    ext x
   100	    constructor
   101	    · rintro ⟨_, ⟨i, rfl⟩, rfl⟩
   102	      exact ⟨i, rfl⟩
   103	    · rintro ⟨i, rfl⟩
   104	      exact ⟨A.row i, ⟨i, rfl⟩, rfl⟩
   105	  rw [prefixRank, Matrix.rank_eq_finrank_span_row, Submodule.map_span, himage]
   106	
   107	/--
   108	The non-pivot coordinate set of `W`, defined by the rank-increase
   109	characterization of pivots.  This is the basis-free encoding approved for
   110	blueprint `def:canonical-complement`;
   111	the paper's Gaussian-elimination presentation is
   112	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:303-320`.
   113	-/
   114	noncomputable def canonicalComplement {n : ℕ}
   115	    (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K)) : Finset (Fin n) :=
   116	  Finset.univ.filter fun j =>
   117	    prefixRank W (j.1 + 1) (Nat.succ_le_of_lt j.2) =
   118	      prefixRank W j.1 j.2.le
   119	
   120	/-- The register submodule is the standard coordinate span on its index set. -/
   121	lemma registerSubmodule_eq_spanSubset (S : Finset ι) :
   122	    registerSubmodule K S = Pi.spanSubset K (S : Set ι) := by
   123	  classical
   124	  rw [registerSubmodule, Pi.spanSubset]
   125	  congr 1
   126	  ext v
   127	  simp [Pi.basisFun_apply, eq_comm]
   128	
   129	/-- Prefix restriction rank is nondecreasing when one coordinate is added. -/
   130	lemma prefixRank_mono_succ {n : ℕ} (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K))
   131	    (k : ℕ) (hk : k + 1 ≤ n) :
   132	    prefixRank W k (Nat.le_trans (Nat.le_succ k) hk) ≤
   133	      prefixRank W (k + 1) hk := by
   134	  let drop := prefixMap (K := K) k (k + 1) (Nat.le_succ k)
   135	  let large := prefixMap (K := K) (k + 1) n hk
   136	  have hcomp : drop.comp large =
   137	      prefixMap (K := K) k n (Nat.le_trans (Nat.le_succ k) hk) := by
   138	    ext x i
   139	    rfl
   140	  rw [prefixRank, prefixRank, ← hcomp, Submodule.map_comp]

   502		$\sum_j \kappa_q(M_{i,j} v_j) = \sum_j K_{M_{i,j}}\, \kappa_q(v_j)$, which
   503		is the $i$-th block row of $\chi_q(M)$ applied to $\kappa_q(v)$.

   506	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:one}
   507		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.trace_basis_eq_one_of_selfDual_normal, MIPStarRE.QPBT.basisCoord_one_of_selfDual_normal}
   508		\leanok
   509		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   510		Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ a self-dual normal basis of
   511		$\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$. Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and the
   512		representation $\kappa(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all-ones
   513		vector in $\F_2^k$.
   514	\end{lemma}
   515	\begin{proof}
   516		\leanok
   517		\uses{lem:downsize_field}
   518		Normality gives $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$ (indices taken cyclically), and
   519		$\tr(b^2) = \tr(b)$ for every $b \in \F_{2^k}$ because squaring permutes the
   520		terms of $\tr(b) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} b^{2^j}$, using $b^{2^k} = b$. Hence all
   521		the values $\tr(e_i)$ coincide. If the common value were $0$, then $\tr$
   522		would vanish identically on $\F_{2^k}$ by linearity; but then item 1 of
   523		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} would give $\kappa(b) =
   524		(\tr(b e_1), \dots, \tr(b e_k)) = 0$ for every $b$, contradicting the
   525		bijectivity of $\kappa$. Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and item 1 of
   526		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} gives
   527		$\kappa(1) = (\tr(e_1), \dots, \tr(e_k)) = (1, \dots, 1)$.
   528	\end{proof}

   530	\begin{definition}[Binary representation of field elements]\label{def:binary-representation}
   531		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.FixedFieldModel.binaryCoordinates, MIPStarRE.QPBT.multiplicationTable, MIPStarRE.QPBT.chi, MIPStarRE.QPBT.binaryCoordinates_mul}
   532		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.binaryCoordinates_basis_mul}
   533		\leanok
   534		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size,
   535			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   536		Let $q = 2^k$ be an admissible field size. For each odd $k$ we fix, once and
   537		for all, a self-dual normal basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   538		$\F_2$ together with its multiplication tables
   539		$\{K_{e_i}\}_{i=1}^k$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis});
   540		the maps $\kappa$ and $\tr$ always refer to this basis. The \emph{binary
   541		representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is the $k$-bit string
   542		$\kappa(a) \in \F_2^k$, the \emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}; the two are
   543		freely identified. Addition of representations is bitwise addition modulo
   544		$2$, and multiplication is determined by the multiplication tables through
   545		\begin{equation}\label{eq:eq-mult}
   546			\kappa(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i\, \kappa(e_i b)
   547			= \sum_{i=1}^k a_i \bigl(K_{e_i}\, \kappa(b)\bigr)\;,
   548		\end{equation}
   549		where $\kappa(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$.
   550		The sums use coordinates $0,\ldots,k-1$; coordinate $r$ corresponds to the
   551		paper's coordinate $r+1$.
   552	\end{definition}

   554	\section{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   555	% Paper label sec:ld-encoding kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   556	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   557	
   558	\begin{definition}[Individual and total degree]\label{def:polynomials-degree}
   559		\uses{def:polyfunc}
   560		An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   561		\[
   562			f(x_1, \dots, x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}^m}
   563			c_\alpha\, x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   564		\]
   565		with coefficients $c_\alpha \in \F_q$; the coefficients are uniquely
   566		determined by $f$, since the $q^m$ monomial functions indexed by
   567		$\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}^m$ span the $q^m$-dimensional space of all
   568		functions $\F_q^m \to \F_q$ and are therefore linearly independent. The
   569		polynomial $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if
   570		$c_\alpha \neq 0$ only when $\alpha_i \le d$ for all $1 \le i \le m$, and
   571		\emph{total degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha \neq 0$ only when
   572		$\sum_i \alpha_i \le d$. (Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are those
   573		of individual degree $1$.
   574		% Relationship to def:polyfunc: polyfunc keeps polynomial representatives,
   575		% so evaluation identifies it with the function classes above only for
   576		% d <= q-1.
   577		Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc} introduces the set $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ of
   578		polynomials in $\F_q[x_1, \dots, x_m]$ of degree at most $d$ in each
   579		variable, identified by their polynomial representatives rather than by the
   580		functions they induce. Evaluation maps $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ onto the set of
   581		$m$-variate polynomials of individual degree at most $\min(d, q-1)$ in the
   582		sense above; for $d \le q-1$ this map is a bijection, while for $d \ge q$
   583		distinct representatives, such as $x_1^q$ and $x_1$, induce the same
   584		function. Statements phrased in terms of $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ retain the
   585		representative convention of Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc}.
   586	\end{definition}
   587	
   588	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz--Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]\label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   589		\lean{MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.schwartzZippel_totalDegree}
   590		\leanok
   591		% Restatement of lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree under the source's label.
   592		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   593		Let $f, g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials of total degree at
   594		most $d$. Then
   595		\[
   596			\Prb_{\bx \sim \F_q^m}[f(\bx) = g(\bx)] \le \frac{d}{q}\;.
   597		\]
   598	\end{lemma}
   599	\begin{proof}
   600		\leanok
   601		\uses{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}
   602		This is Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}, stated and proved in
   603		Chapter~\ref{chap:preliminaries}; it is restated here under the label used
   604		by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   605	\end{proof}
   606	
   607	\begin{remark}\label{rem:schwartz-zippel-restated}
   608		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel} restates the total-degree bound of
   609		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree} under the label used by
   610		\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. The individual-degree consequence,
   611		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-individual}, shows that distinct elements of
   612		$\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ agree on at most an $md/q$ fraction of the points of
   613		$\F_q^m$; the analysis of the Pauli basis test uses the bound in this
   614		individual-degree form.
   615	\end{remark}
   616	
   617	The Schwartz--Zippel lemma implies that low-degree polynomials form an
   618	error-correcting code with good distance, the \emph{low-degree code} (a special
   619	case of the generalized Reed--Muller code).
   620	
   621	\begin{definition}[Low-degree encoding]\label{def:low-degree-encoding}
   622		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.lowDegreeEncoding, MIPStarRE.QPBT.lowDegreeEnc}
   623		\leanok
   624		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   625		Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$. For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$
   626		define the $m$-variate multilinear polynomial over $\F_q$
   627		\[
   628			\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)
   629			= \prod_{i : y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i : y_i = 0} (1 - x_i)\;,
   630		\]
   631		identifying $\{0,1\}$ with a subset of $\F_q$. Restricted to the subcube
   632		$\{0,1\}^m$, the polynomial $\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}$ vanishes everywhere except
   633		at $x = y$, where it equals $1$. For $a \in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates
   634		of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ (identifying $\{0,1\}^m$ with
   635		$\{1, \dots, M\}$ by the lexicographic ordering). The \emph{low-degree
   636		encoding of $a$} is the multilinear polynomial $g_a : \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   637		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   638		\begin{equation}\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   639			g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\;.
   640		\end{equation}
   641		For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ one has $g_a(y) = a_y$, and $g_a$ has total
   642		degree at most $m$.
   643	\end{definition}
   644	
   645	\begin{definition}[Indicator vector and linearity of the encoding]\label{def:indicator-vector}
   646		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.indicatorVec, MIPStarRE.QPBT.lowDegreeEnc_eq_dotProduct}
   647		\leanok
   648		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   649		For $x \in \F_q^m$, the \emph{indicator vector} is
   650		\[
   651			\mathrm{ind}_m(x)
   652			= \bigl(\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\bigr)_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} \in \F_q^M\;.
   653		\]
   654		With this notation the low-degree encoding satisfies, for every
   655		$a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$,
   656		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   657		\begin{equation}\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   658			g_a(x) = a \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(x)\;;
   659		\end{equation}
   660		in particular the map $a \mapsto g_a$ is $\F_q$-linear.
   661	\end{definition}
   662	
   663	Since encodings $g_a$ are multilinear, hence of total degree at most $m$, two
   664	encodings of distinct strings agree on at most an $m/q$ fraction of points of
   665	$\F_q^m$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel}.
   666	
   667	\begin{definition}[Decoding maps]\label{def:decoding-map}
   668		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.decodeAt, MIPStarRE.QPBT.decodeBool, MIPStarRE.QPBT.decodeAt_lowDegreeEnc}
   669		\leanok
   670		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding}
   671		For $H \subseteq \F_q$, the \emph{decoding map} $\mathrm{Dec}_H$ takes as
   672		input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and returns the vector
   673		$a \in \F_q^M$ defined by: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, set $a_y = g(y)$ if
   674		$g(y) \in H$, and $a_y = 0$ otherwise. For all $a \in H^M$ one has
   675		$\mathrm{Dec}_H(g_a) = a$. We write $\mathrm{Dec}(\cdot)$ for the boolean
   676		decoding map $\mathrm{Dec}_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.
   677	\end{definition}
